Recently, I posted a story here about Walter Scott. A man who had fallen into the kafkaesque-clutches of the family court system. Begging the judge for mercy, he asked, "how am I supposed to live [if everything I earn goes to my ex]?"

Sad and depressing stuff. So let's talk about something that's uplifting. How should you live? What should you do in order to find happiness?

It's an important question. People who don't make a conscious effort to address this question will end up rudderless, following the random currents of chance and emotion. Never really in control, if they just happen to find happiness, it will be literally blind luck. Surely we can do better than this!

I have a book on the topic and the title is very close to what Walter Scott asked the judge, so I thought it was a nice segue. How to Live, or a life of Montaigne in one question and twenty attempts at an answer. It's a biography of the 16th century nobleman, Michel de Montaigne. He gives 20 answers to the question, "how should you live" including:

  • Pay attention (that is, be awake and conscious)

  • Question everything (devote yourself to knowledge)

  • Wake from the sleep of habit (shake shit up - do something you've never done before)

  • Do something no one has done before (this, I think is a quintessential source of happiness for men)

It occurs to me that I have spent a lot of time and effort in my life chasing women. I'm not complaining here. This is just introspection. I've followed the path that most men followed. I've been happy too, at times. But I see now that it was the rudderless, blind-luck kind of happiness. I've been lucky to date a few quality women, but this is not the best strategy going forward.

If you can really and truly stop focusing on women (and that including stop complaining about them) then MGTOW is really kind of a blessing. Surely a deliberate, conscious effort to seek happiness will be more rewarding than being led about by your mating instinct (even if you remain open to sex when convenient).

So what do you do? What is your philosophy on life and your plan to be happy?

For me, the four items that I listed above are good guideposts. I think I'm awake now. I'm paying attention - some people say, "taking the red pill." I've renewed my devotion to learning. Haven't started back to school yet but that's in the works. I've been trying a few new hobbies, in an attempt to break old habits, though I haven't found something I really like yet.

Anyone have any insights they want to add?
Okay, so how are you supposed to live?

What's great about MGTOW is that you are free to pursue near anything you want. Myself, I like history, and I like learning and teaching.

My philosophy first begins with an observation that most 'new' ideas are in fact either a recycle of very old ideas, or at best modest improvements. CS Lewis gives the example of Confucius teaching "Don't do to others what you don't want them to do to you," Christ later imporving this by teaching "Do to others as you would have them do to you," and no further improvement has been forthcoming on this general idea for millenia. The OP, also, indirectly affirms the idea when quoting de Montaigne.

I think we have been taught some negative knowledge in regard to what knowledge itself is, and indeed what manhood is. I have dedicated myself to unlearning the falsehoods in contemporary philosophy, in the hope of finding real truth. Once you do this, you find out pretty quikly that "forward thinking" ideologies are in fact throwbacks to ideas that already failed multiple times in history, and that the truth tends to reassert itself despite many historyical attempts to repress it.

Right now, we are sitting in a pretty intersting part of history; we are seeing another opporunity to overturn some of the great lies of our time, feminism being just one head of this particular hydra. What makes me happy is being a part of the turning.

What makes me happy is being a part of the turning.

For me, I find that activism and political causes in general orient me toward an external locus of control. What I mean by that is, I get so invested in hoping that something happens (a candidate getting elected, or like what you said, feminism being overturned) that if it doesn't go the way I wanted, I'm disappointed and feel powerless.

So for me, I want to retain power over what I'm doing. When I fail, I want to fail at something that I can go back again and succeed at.
